speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment with regard to the release of treated wastewater from the Fukushima nuclear plant into the Sea by Japan (a) what measures are in place to ensure the safety of our food products, especially seafood, imported from Japan; and (b) whether the Ministry has assessed the potential impact on Singapore's surrounding waters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment with regard to the impending release of treated radioactive water from the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant into the ocean (a) whether the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) will review the safety of seafood imports from Japan; and (b) what actions will SFA take when an imported food is found to have elevated levels of tritium or other radionuclide levels.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To ensure food safety, food imported into Singapore is subjected to SFA's surveillance and monitoring regime, which includes radiation surveillance.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Food products that fail SFA's inspections and tests will not be allowed for sale.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA also keeps abreast of international developments and expert reports from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and foreign food safety authorities to augment our surveillance and monitoring regime.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Since 2019, NEA has been closely monitoring Singapore's waters as part of NEA's environmental baseline radiation monitoring programme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA and NEA will continue to monitor closely radiation levels in our food imports and our environment respectively.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that NEA operates a network of about 40 ambient radiation monitoring stations in and around Singapore, which provide a daily update on radiation levels.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, may I ask if the Ministry of Sustainability and Environment (MSE) has any plans to increase the frequency of monitoring to more than once a day or to include more monitoring stations?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second question is a request for the readings to be made known to the public; and third, does MSE have any processes presently to monitor the presence of tritium in our environment?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Make known to public on the radiation levels.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Any process presently to monitor the presence of tritium in our environment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And we do include readings on radiation and, if necessary, we will make some of these known if we need the public to be aware.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Because these monitors actually collect a lot of data, so, we do not think that it is necessary to highlight one of them, unless it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And we have in the past, for example, when it comes to haze, we do highlight certain readings when we think that it is necessary for the public to take action.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Otherwise, there will be a lot of data that may inundate the public and actually may not have the desired impact.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For some indicators, we do intend to increase the number of monitors, but I will just assure the Member that we will look into the overall requirements of environmental protection and assess our capability from time to time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, I would like to ask if SFA tests all imported food products coming from high-risk locations where there are potential nuclear contamination issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, what would be the recourse for consumers who suspect that they have bought or consumed a product that contains high radionucleic levels?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We take a risk-based approach when it comes to food safety and these risks could be many different types of risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It can be from nuclear activities, nuclear active materials, it can be contamination from the environment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are inundated actually with many, many different types of risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I would not want Members to go away thinking that nuclear contamination is the only thing that we are concerned with or this is an issue that we are concerned about right now.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As I have mentioned earlier in my reply, we have actually been monitoring a whole host of risks and you can see that SFA, from time to time, does take action against food items that do not meet our requirements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, this regime will continue and, of course, we will watch the situation with the discharge of Fukushima wastewater carefully.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also rely on international assessments and we do exchange data and intelligence with other food safety authorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister said that the discharge of wastewater is unlikely to impact the waters around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But can I ask the Minister if NEA or SFA is monitoring whether the water around the areas where our sources of seafood come from is being monitored to assess whether or not it will impact Singapore?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Of course, we will monitor reports coming from those areas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As you see, we do not have jurisdiction in those areas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is really not very realistic for us to expect NEA to be monitoring the quality of waters several thousand miles away from Singapore.
